reference.source: Postgraduate Haematology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: Caused by reduced or absent alpha-globin production, usually from deletions of one or more of the four alpha-globin genes (HBA1 and HBA2)

Severity tracks the number of functional alpha genes: loss of one is silent, loss of two gives thalassaemia trait, loss of three gives HbH disease, and loss of all four causes Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis
Trait produces a mild microcytic hypochromic anaemia that is easily mistaken for iron deficiency but with normal or raised iron stores
HbH disease causes a chronic haemolytic anaemia with splenomegaly, and HbH inclusions can be demonstrated in red cells with supravital staining
Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis (four-gene loss) is generally fatal in utero or at birth and carries serious maternal risks in pregnancy
Diagnosis combines red-cell indices, exclusion of iron deficiency, haemoglobin analysis (which may be near-normal in trait), and DNA studies for the alpha-gene deletions
Management ranges from none in trait, through folate support and judicious transfusion in HbH disease, to prenatal counselling for at-risk couples
reference.pathophysiology: Alpha thalassaemia arises from decreased or absent synthesis of alpha-globin chains, most commonly from deletions involving the duplicated alpha-globin genes HBA1 and HBA2 (non-deletional point mutations also occur). Because alpha chains are shared by fetal and adult haemoglobins, deficiency creates an excess of the partner chains: excess gamma chains in fetal life form Hb Bart's, and excess beta chains after birth form HbH. These abnormal tetramers are unstable and have very high oxygen affinity, so they precipitate and damage red cells and deliver oxygen poorly, producing ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis in proportion to the degree of alpha-chain deficit.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and red-cell indices showing microcytosis and hypochromia
Blood film for target cells and, in HbH disease, features of haemolysis
Iron studies to distinguish from iron deficiency
Supravital staining to demonstrate HbH inclusions
Haemoglobin high-performance liquid chromatography or electrophoresis
DNA analysis for alpha-globin gene deletions and point mutations
redFlags: Hydropic fetus or severe fetal anaemia suggesting Hb Bart's, with maternal pre-eclampsia risk
Rapidly worsening anaemia during infection or with oxidant exposure in HbH disease
Transfusional or absorptive iron overload with end-organ dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Silent carriers and trait have a normal life expectancy, HbH disease is generally compatible with a good quality of life with supportive care though severity varies, and four-gene deletion (Hb Bart's) is usually lethal perinatally unless intrauterine intervention is undertaken.
pitfalls: Diagnosing iron deficiency and giving prolonged iron therapy when microcytosis is actually thalassaemic
Assuming a normal haemoglobin analysis excludes alpha thalassaemia, since trait may show no abnormal band
Overlooking the need for prenatal counselling when both partners carry alpha-gene deletions
Precipitating haemolysis in HbH disease with oxidant drugs or by not treating intercurrent infection
